title: Why Private Equity's Software Bet Is Going to Zero | The Weekly Wrap

metadata.title: Why Private Equity's Software Bet Is Going to Zero | The Weekly Wrap

summary: Eisman links FICO's loss of exclusivity to regulator antagonism and examines software buyouts financed in a low-rate era. His residual-equity example is arithmetically sound if enterprise value halves and debt is unchanged, but it does not establish that public equity drawdowns proxy private enterprise values. The precise refinancing cash demand is not a mathematical necessity. He also distinguishes oil supply shocks from the Fed's broader inflation role and describes the vintage-delinquency work behind his crisis trade.
assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Model residual equity and refinancing explicitly.
Use vintage credit data rather than stories to identify deterioration.
tools_and_charts: Five software buyout purchase prices and debt ratios
transcript_cautions: Captions render Anaplan, Thoma Bravo, Permira and Galcap inconsistently; entity names were normalized only when context is clear.
The hypothetical equity arithmetic does not establish the assumptions for the actual named deals.

claims.reason: The statement does not specify an objective threshold, horizon or counterfactual that permits a determinate outcome grade.

claims.claim: For a $1 billion buyout with unchanged $500 million debt, a fall in enterprise value to $500 million eliminates residual equity even if operations remain profitable.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Verify EV and debt premises before applying to any real company.
claims.reason: This conditional relationship follows from the stated assumptions; it does not establish that the assumptions hold empirically.
claims.next_check: Verify EV and debt premises before applying to any real company.

assumptions: EV falls from $1 billion to $500 million
Debt remains $500 million; no cash adjustment
evidence_basis.proof: Equity = max(EV - debt, 0) = zero. Operating profitability does not prevent valuation compression.

assumptions: EV falls from $1 billion to $500 million
Debt remains $500 million; no cash adjustment
proof.derivation: Equity = max(EV - debt, 0) = zero. Operating profitability does not prevent valuation compression.

claims.claim: Medallia was taken over by lenders in August after a failed software buyout; Pluralsight is cited as an earlier example.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect original restructuring documents and realized sponsor recoveries for both deals.
claims.reason: Medallia confirms transfer to lender-linked investors and recapitalization, but the inspected release does not quantify the prior sponsor's recovery; Pluralsight has not been independently inspected here.

evidence.title: Medallia Closes Transaction to Fuel Company's Next Chapter
evidence.finding: Completed lender recapitalization reduced debt, raised $150 million and transferred ownership to Blackstone-, Apollo- and FSK-led investors.

claims.next_check: Inspect original restructuring documents and realized sponsor recoveries for both deals.

claims.claim: The Fed cannot repair an oil supply shock, but persistent oil inflation can spread and justify demand restraint through higher rates.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate physical supply control from demand, currency and expectation channels.
claims.reason: The inflation-growth tradeoff and secondary effects are supported. Saying rate changes have zero impact on oil prices is too absolute because demand and exchange-rate channels can affect prices.

evidence.title: The Changing Sensitivity of Interest Rates to Oil Supply News
evidence.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
evidence.finding: Oil supply shocks create inflation-growth tradeoffs; policy can dampen activity and expectations, and oil-price responses reflect both supply and demand.

claims.next_check: Separate physical supply control from demand, currency and expectation channels.
